title: Taint Shared Content
summary: Taint Shared Content covers any attempt to place malicious code inside a shared location so that another user runs it, including network drives, collaboration sites, and internal code repositories. The adversary rarely attacks a machine directly. Instead they append or prepend code to a legitimate binary and redirect its entry point, plant a document that carries a script, or replace a folder with a shortcut file that hides the payload and then opens the real folder so the user's expected action still happens. Execution therefore occurs under the victim's own account on the victim's own host, and the file server records only a write. Detection leans on integrity monitoring of shares and repositories, unexpected writes by accounts that do not own the content, and process trees in which an office document or shortcut launches a script interpreter or command shell.

beginner.definition: Shared content is any file that many people can open, such as a folder on a network drive or a project in a code repository. Tainting means adding hidden malicious code to those files. When a colleague opens the file, the attacker's code runs on that colleague's computer. This is a technique in its own right, used to reach other systems.
beginner.whyItMatters: Shared folders and code repositories are trusted places. People open files there without thinking, because a teammate put them there. One infected file can reach hundreds of computers, and it can be opened again after cleaning. The attacker does not need a password for each machine, because the victim runs the code for them. That makes shared storage a very efficient way to spread.
howItWorks: The attacker gains write access to a shared folder, document library, or internal code repository.
They add malicious code to a normal file, such as a document, script, or program.
A colleague opens the file, believing it came from a trusted team member.
The hidden part runs and contacts the attacker, giving them a foothold on that machine.
In one variation, a folder shortcut file looks like the real folder and hides the payload.
Defenders detect unexpected writes to shares and files that start command shells when opened.
beginner.example: Imagine a shared kitchen where everyone leaves food in one fridge with a note saying help yourself. One person adds a dish that looks exactly like the usual meal but contains something spoiled. Everyone who takes a portion becomes ill, and the dish is refilled each morning. Shared folders work the same way: the container is trusted, so nobody checks the contents, and the problem spreads with every helping.
takeaways: Treat shared drives and repositories as untrusted and scan the files there.
Watch for unusual writes to shares and for documents that start scripts.
Clean the shared file and the affected hosts together, or the problem returns.

objectives: Explain how malicious content reaches other systems through shared storage.
Describe common variants such as binary infection and folder shortcut tricks.
Identify telemetry that reveals unexpected writes to shared locations.
Explain how process creation logs link an opened file to a suspicious child process.
Outline the controls that reduce the spread of tainted shared content.
